questions.q: Club A has 40 students: 16 like Math ($A$), 20 are in the AI Club ($B$) and 12 are in both. What is $P(A \mid B)$?
questions.explain: Conditioning shrinks the universe to the 20 AI-Club students: $P(A \mid B) = 12/20 = 0.60$. $0.30 = 12/40$ forgets to change the denominator, $0.75 = 12/16$ is $P(B \mid A)$, and $0.40$ is the unconditional $P(A)$.

questions.q: In the same club, why is $P(B \mid A) = 0.75$ different from $P(A \mid B) = 0.60$?
options: Because one of the two formulas uses a different numerator
Both share the numerator $P(A \cap B)$ but divide by different denominators, $P(A)$ vs. $P(B)$
They should be equal; the difference is sampling noise
questions.explain: $P(A \mid B) = P(A \cap B)/P(B)$ and $P(B \mid A) = P(A \cap B)/P(A)$. Same overlap, different new universe — they agree only when $P(A) = P(B)$.

questions.q: Club B has 40 students: 16 like Math, 20 are in the AI Club, 8 are in both. What does conditioning on "in the AI Club" do?
options: Leaves it unchanged: $P(A \mid B) = 8/20 = 0.40 = P(A)$ — the events are independent
Raises the chance of liking Math to $0.50$
Makes it undefined because the overlap is small
questions.explain: $P(A \mid B) = 8/20 = 0.40$ and $P(A) = 16/40 = 0.40$. The clue tells you nothing new — that is independence.

questions.q: If $P(A \cap B) = 0.15$ and $P(B) = 0.5$, what is $P(A \mid B)$?
questions.explain: $P(A \mid B) = P(A \cap B)/P(B) = 0.15/0.5 = 0.30$. Multiplying ($0.075$) or ignoring the condition ($0.15$) are common slips.
